strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General. Under that framing, unifying eight fragmented fall-detection datasets into a common taxonomy and standardized protocols is a useful contribution even without a novel model.

The benchmark has meaningful scale and diversity relative to individual fall datasets: approximately 14 hours of unique recordings, 42 hours including synchronized views, 101 subjects, and 29 camera views.

Separating transient actions such as falling or sitting down from persistent states such as fallen or sitting is practically motivated and supports more informative evaluation than conventional binary fall labels.

The OOPS-Fall evaluation exposes a large staged-to-wild gap that would remain hidden by conventional within-dataset testing. The contrast between I3D and VideoMAE representations is an interesting baseline finding.

The paper evaluates multiple granularities, including ten-class recognition, fall, fallen, their union, and temporal segmentation, and reports balanced accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F1, edit score, and segmental F1.
The limitations and societal-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges demographic bias, surveillance and privacy risks, false alarms, and the limited coverage of the wild test set.
weaknesses: The central dataset construction is insufficiently documented. The paper gives no annotation guidelines or operational class definitions, number or expertise of annotators, boundary-labeling rules, quality-control process, inter-annotator agreement, or adjudication procedure. These omissions are consequential because distinctions such as fall versus fallen and lie-down versus lying are inherently ambiguous.

OOPS-Fall is under-specified: the exact positive/negative counts, sampling and filtering rules, subject and scenario composition, segment duration distribution, duplicate removal, verification protocol, and annotation reliability are absent. It is therefore unclear whether the measured gap reflects staged-to-wild generalization, changes in action/context composition, or selection artifacts.

The motivating emphasis on medically critical fallen states and long-lie episodes is not validated in the wild. OOPS-Fall is annotated only as fall/no-fall, so the benchmark does not test real-world fallen-state recognition, duration of incapacitation, or the elderly population central to the stated application.

The cross-view protocol may share synchronized recordings—and thus the same subjects, actions, timing, and scene content—between training and test cameras. For EDF/OCCU, for example, one synchronized view is used for training and the other for testing. Other nominal cross-view splits instead change rooms or subjects. Consequently, the protocol mixes distinct notions of view generalization and can yield optimistic or incomparable results unless recording-level separation and confounds are analyzed.

Reproducibility and availability are unclear: the supplied manuscript contains blank 'OmniFall:' and 'Code:' entries, while many numerical results and backbone settings are deferred to an unavailable supplementary document. Redistribution rights, licensing constraints, and access procedures for the constituent videos and derived annotations are not specified.

The ethics and governance of curating genuine accident footage need substantially more detail, including the OOPS license terms for derivative annotations or redistribution, privacy handling, consent expectations, treatment of identifiable people and potentially distressing footage, and intended access controls.

The experimental evidence is limited to three frozen representations with one lightweight classifier, with no comparison to representative published fall-detection systems, pose-based baselines, modern end-to-end video models, or simple per-dataset versus unified-training controls. This limits the benchmark's positioning and the conclusions about what enables robust generalization.

No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or statistical tests are reported. Several constituent test sets are very small, so apparent differences between backbones may not be reliable. The definition of the 'Overall' aggregation across datasets is also unclear.

The domain-shift analysis is largely qualitative. Applying a Fréchet distance to each backbone's features creates backbone-dependent spaces that are not directly comparable, and the t-SNE/H-NNE plots do not substantiate causal claims that simpler I3D representations explain better wild performance.

There are attribution and presentation problems: MS-TCN++ is cited using the original MS-TCN reference, model naming alternates between VMAE-Pre and VMAE-K400-Pre, and several strong interpretations—such as supervised pretraining inducing view invariance—are not isolated experimentally. Overall, the benchmark idea is promising, but the missing annotation validation, ambiguous protocols, and insufficiently specified wild set support a slight preference for rejection in the current form.

strengths: The paper addresses a socially important computer-vision problem and correctly emphasizes that strong performance on staged fall datasets may not translate to genuine accidents.

As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, harmonizing eight datasets into a ten-class taxonomy, including transient actions and persistent states, could provide useful infrastructure for cross-dataset research.

The cross-subject, cross-view, and staged-to-wild protocols expose meaningful differences between controlled and uncontrolled evaluation. In particular, the low OOPS-Fall sensitivity of the VideoMAE models is an informative result that aggregate in-domain accuracy would obscure.

The benchmark reports several complementary metrics and includes temporal-segmentation results, rather than restricting evaluation to trimmed binary classification. weaknesses: The central dataset contribution is insufficiently validated. There is no annotation manual or operational definition for semantically difficult boundaries such as fall versus lie down and fallen versus lying; nor are annotator counts, training, quality-control procedures, inter-annotator agreement, or disagreement resolution reported. Consequently, the reliability of the new dense labels cannot be assessed.

OOPS-Fall curation is described only as filtering original tags followed by manual verification. The paper omits the positive/negative counts, selection criteria, excluded cases, source distribution, annotation procedure, class balance, demographic composition, duplicate handling, and representative failure modes. OOPS contains general unintentional actions, so evidence is needed that this subset represents genuine human falls relevant to the stated elder-care motivation.

The cross-view protocol may leak synchronized instances: one camera view of an event can be used for training while another view of the same event appears in testing. This evaluates view transfer for known event instances, not generalization jointly across recordings, subjects, and views, and can substantially overstate deployment generalization. The exact recording separation used for train, validation, and test is not documented.

Reproducibility and availability are currently inadequate. The OmniFall and Code entries on the first page are blank, licenses or redistribution permissions for the included datasets and accident videos are not established, and essential preprocessing details—clip construction, temporal sampling, feature extraction, label collapsing, oversampling implementation, random seeds, and the definition of the reported overall aggregates—are missing.

The experimental evidence is too narrow for establishing a benchmark. It compares only frozen I3D/VideoMAE representations with one temporal classifier and MS-TCN++, without established fall-detection systems, simple motion/posture baselines, fine-tuning, domain-generalization methods, or leave-one-dataset-out evaluation. Results have no repeated runs, uncertainty intervals, or significance analysis.

Some essential evidence is deferred to an unavailable supplement: the numerical FVD values, additional feature settings, and the full VideoMAE-Pre table. Naming is also inconsistent between VideoMAE-Pre and VMAE-K400-Pre. Thus several comparative claims cannot be checked from the supplied manuscript.

The domain-shift analysis is not rigorous enough to support its interpretations. Sampling 5,000 pooled features is underspecified for datasets with far fewer segments, FVD estimation and uncertainty are not reported, and t-SNE/H-NNE plots do not by themselves establish that clustering is caused by domain rather than class imbalance, clip construction, or duplicated multiview events.

The OOPS-Fall temporal-segmentation experiment is unclear because the paper says OOPS-Fall has only fall/no-fall segment labels, whereas MS-TCN++ is trained with the ten-class taxonomy. It never explains how predictions and ground truth are mapped for F1@IoU and edit score, making Table 4 difficult to interpret or reproduce.

The clinical and deployment framing is stronger than the evidence. Most training subjects are young actors, OOPS-Fall is not shown to represent older adults or long-lie episodes, and the experiments do not evaluate alarm latency, false alarms per hour, calibration, continuous-stream operation, or demographic disparities.

Because this is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper, the lack of a credible annotation audit, clearly leakage-resistant protocols, and demonstrable data/code availability directly undermines the primary contribution. The aggregation and staged-to-wild idea have merit, but the current evidence does not support acceptance.

strengths: This is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution. Unifying eight heterogeneous fall-detection datasets under a common ten-class, temporally dense taxonomy is practically valuable and enables comparisons that incompatible original annotations previously prevented.

The distinction between transient actions (e.g., falling or lying down) and persistent states (especially fallen) is well motivated by the clinical importance of long-lie episodes and makes the benchmark more useful than a simple fall/non-fall collection.

The staged-to-wild evaluation using OOPS-Fall addresses an important weakness of the field. The large sensitivity drop on genuine accident footage provides compelling evidence that performance on staged laboratory data can substantially overstate real-world robustness.

The benchmark includes complementary cross-subject and cross-view protocols, multiple evaluation granularities, domain-distance analyses, and temporal-segmentation experiments. Results across I3D and VideoMAE representations expose meaningful differences between in-domain accuracy and out-of-domain generalization.

The manuscript is generally clear and visually effective, and it gives unusually concrete dataset-specific split definitions. The limitations and societal-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges demographic bias, privacy concerns, false alarms, and the risks of reduced human oversight.
weaknesses: The central annotations are insufficiently documented for a benchmark paper. The manuscript does not specify the number or expertise of annotators, labeling instructions and boundary definitions, quality-control process, adjudication, or inter-annotator agreement. OOPS-Fall curation is described only as filtering and manual verification; exact class counts, durations, selection criteria, ambiguity handling, and annotation reliability are missing.

The relationship between OOPS-Fall's binary fall/no-fall labels and the ten-class taxonomy is unclear, particularly for the reported MS-TCN++ temporal-segmentation metrics. The paper should state exactly which labels and mappings are used for every OOPS-Fall experiment and how segment boundaries are defined.

Some evaluation protocols mix different notions of generalization. For example, the GMDCSA cross-view split appears to change subjects and locations rather than only cameras, while single-view datasets participate only in training. The paper should clarify these confounds and how validation examples are separated when training and validation use the same view.

The experimental evidence lacks uncertainty estimates, repeated runs, per-class/test-set sample counts, and comparisons with stronger contemporary or end-to-end baselines. It is also unclear whether reported 'overall' metrics are pooled or averaged across datasets. These omissions make some backbone-level conclusions more confident than the evidence supports.

There is a concrete inconsistency in the discussion of I3D: the text claims binary-fall specificity remains above 0.98 across all domains, whereas Table 2 reports OOPS-Fall specificity of 0.79 and 0.63 for the two protocols. Interpretations based on specificity and deployment readiness should be corrected accordingly.

Reproducibility and governance need improvement. The displayed OmniFall and code fields contain no usable links, licensing and redistribution permissions for the unified release are not established, and possible overlap between web-sourced OOPS videos and large pretraining corpora is not investigated. The claimed real-world relevance should also be qualified because general OOPS accidents may not represent elderly residential falls.

Several analytical claims are exploratory rather than firmly demonstrated: t-SNE/H-NNE geometry is used to explain generalization, and apparent performance differences are attributed to pretraining properties without controlled ablations. The MS-TCN++ attribution also appears to cite the original MS-TCN reference rather than the specific MS-TCN++ method.

strengths: The work addresses an important computer-vision problem with clear practical relevance: staged fall-detection benchmarks are small and poorly representative of deployment conditions, while collecting genuine falls is difficult and ethically sensitive.

Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, this is more appropriately assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper than as Algorithms/General. Under that framing, unifying eight staged datasets, reannotating them with a common 16-class frame-level taxonomy, and defining cross-subject, cross-view, and cross-domain protocols are potentially valuable contributions.

The three-domain design is thoughtful. Staged data provide structured motion, synthetic data provide controllable appearance variation, and the 818-video OF-ItW collection provides a substantially more realistic evaluation target. Supporting both classification and temporal segmentation further increases potential utility.

The paper provides useful baseline evidence across frozen I3D, VideoMAE, and SigLIP2 representations, including feature-space analyses, cross-domain classification, timeline segmentation, and synthetic cross-age/cross-BMI tests. The result that synthetic-only training attains 64.2 fall F1 on OF-ItW versus 60.5–61.2 for staged training is interesting and practically relevant.

The appendix documents source-dataset permissions, split identities, synthetic prompt factors, computational resources, and annotation tooling. The limitations and societal-impact discussion appropriately acknowledges surveillance risks, false alarms, generator bias, and the need for real-care validation.
weaknesses: The reported dataset scale is internally inconsistent. The abstract claims 80 hours, the introduction and appendix claim 82 hours including multi-view recordings, but the per-dataset totals in Table 1 sum to approximately 61.6 hours (about 42.1 staged + 2.65 wild + 16.9 synthetic). Section 4.2 separately states 61.5 hours for OF-Staged and 49.8 hours for CMDFall, whereas Table 1 reports approximately 42.0 and 28.0 hours, respectively. These discrepancies affect a central benchmark claim and must be reconciled.

The experimental methodology contains a consequential contradiction. Section 4 states that VideoMAE-K400 is fine-tuned end-to-end, while the appendix says classification uses precomputed features followed by a lightweight temporal transformer. The paper also does not define the classification sample unit, temporal windowing or aggregation, class balancing, transformer dimensions, or checkpoint-selection procedure. Thus, Tables 2–5 are not presently reproducible or even unambiguously attributable to the stated model.

Annotation validation is insufficient for a benchmark whose main contribution is dense standardized labeling. Nearly all videos receive a second review, but no independently double-annotated subset, inter-annotator agreement, boundary-tolerance analysis, per-class quality audit, or quantitative error estimate is reported. Labels are transferred between synchronized views rather than independently checked, despite possible view-dependent occlusion and synchronization errors.

The evidential breadth is limited. Classification uses only one representation/model pipeline, segmentation primarily one supervised method, and no strong recent fall-detection systems are reimplemented. Results are apparently from single runs without confidence intervals or significance tests; consequently, conclusions based on small differences such as 64.2 versus 65.6 F1 are overstated.

OF-ItW is derived from OOPS rather than newly collected genuine-accident footage, making the claimed novelty depend mainly on filtering and relabeling. The manuscript does not sufficiently specify fall inclusion/exclusion rules, source distributions, duplicate or near-duplicate removal, or possible overlap with video pretraining data. It also calls OF-ItW test-only while proposing a public 10/20/70 split, but gives no hidden-test server or other mechanism preventing repeated test-set tuning.

The synthetic demographic experiments validate prompt categories rather than verified visual attributes. There is no audit that Wan 2.2 reliably realizes the requested age, ethnicity, skin tone, or BMI, nor analysis of artifacts, generation failure rates, filtering rates, or annotator judgments of realism. Claims of controlled demographic coverage and bias assessment are therefore stronger than the evidence supports.

The domain-distance analysis is under-specified and partly confounded by class, environment, and clip-length distributions. Applying a Fréchet-style metric to several feature families is not accompanied by sampling, normalization, covariance-estimation, or uncertainty details, while t-SNE/H-NNE plots mainly demonstrate dataset separability and do not establish semantic domain proximity.

Benchmark availability and governance remain uncertain: the project-page field is blank, code and data are promised only after acceptance, several constituent datasets are non-commercial or permission-based, and the paper does not explain whether annotations, videos, or download scripts can legally be redistributed under one usable license. Together with the quantitative and methodological inconsistencies, these issues prevent a convincing reproducible benchmark case in the current version.

strengths: As a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, the paper addresses an important computer-vision problem: existing fall datasets are fragmented, staged, and difficult to compare. Harmonizing eight datasets into a 16-class frame-level taxonomy and defining cross-subject, cross-view, and cross-domain protocols could be useful to the community.

The benchmark has meaningful scale and complementary domains: approximately 33 hours of unique single-view footage, roughly 80 hours when synchronized views are counted, 12,000 synthetic videos, and 818 curated in-the-wild clips. Distinguishing transient falls from the persistent fallen state is practically well motivated.

The paper documents source-dataset licenses or permissions, provides detailed staged and synthetic split definitions, evaluates both classification and temporal segmentation, and includes a thoughtful limitations and societal-impact discussion covering surveillance, false alarms, demographic bias, and deployment risks.
weaknesses: The dataset's central quality claim is insufficiently validated. Approximately ten annotators were used, but the paper reports no independent double-annotation rate, inter-annotator agreement, boundary-tolerance analysis, class-wise audit, or measured error rate. Saying that nearly all videos received a two-pass review does not establish reliable frame-level labels. Moreover, labels are transferred from one selected camera to synchronized views, although visibility and occlusion can differ substantially across views.

The experimental description is internally inconsistent. Section 4 says that VideoMAE-K400 is fine-tuned end-to-end, whereas Appendix A.5 describes frozen extracted features followed by a lightweight temporal transformer. Table 2 is titled as training on CMDFall under both CS and CV, but it provides no CMDFall-CV result, while the accompanying text attributes an 80.9% CV accuracy to that experiment even though 80.9% appears in Table 3 for training on the full OF-Staged collection. These discrepancies impede reproducibility and confidence in the results.

The headline conclusion that synthetic data can match or surpass real staged footage is substantially broader than the evidence. It rests primarily on one architecture and one target collection, with Fall F1 differences of only about 3 points between synthetic and staged training and 1.4 points between synthetic-only and combined training. There are no repeated runs, confidence intervals, significance tests, alternative modern video models, or analyses controlling for training volume and the strong scene-composition confound noted by the authors themselves.

OF-In-the-Wild is curated from OOPS rather than collected and validated specifically for fall detection. The paper does not adequately establish that all clips represent genuine falls relevant to care deployment, analyze source or near-duplicate leakage, characterize subject demographics and fall mechanisms, or compare this sample with the intended elderly-care population. Calling it a rigorous real-world benchmark is therefore premature.

The proposed public, test-only benchmark lacks a credible long-term evaluation mechanism: labels appear intended for public release, and the manuscript does not describe a hidden test server, submission limits, or a sequestered test set. Repeated development against these 818 clips would quickly compromise their value as an unbiased target-domain test. Redistribution and consent/privacy issues for identifiable genuine-accident internet footage also require more careful treatment beyond citing the OOPS dataset license.

The synthetic demographic protocols assume that prompt attributes such as age, ethnicity, skin tone, and BMI are faithfully rendered by Wan 2.2, but no human or automated attribute audit supports that assumption. Generator failures, correlations between demographic prompts and age-specific environments, and stereotyped appearance cues could dominate the reported cross-attribute results. The generation procedure also omits important sampling parameters and output-quality statistics, despite claiming reproducibility.

The dataset search is already dated for an ECCV 2026 submission: it was performed in August 2023, searches only PubMed and Google Scholar for surveys published from 2015–2023, and does not directly search primary dataset papers. Thus, the framing of OmniFall as comprehensive is not adequately supported. Overall, the potentially valuable curation effort is outweighed by unresolved benchmark-validity, evaluation, ethics, and reproducibility concerns.

strengths: Although no contribution type is explicitly declared, this is best assessed as a Datasets/Benchmarks paper. Under that framing, the combination of eight harmonized staged datasets, 12,000 synthetic videos, and 818 genuine-accident videos is a substantial and relevant contribution to computer vision for healthcare.

The unified 16-class, frame-level taxonomy supports both video classification and temporal segmentation, including the clinically important distinction between the transient fall event and the persistent fallen state. Standardized cross-subject and cross-view splits address a genuine weakness in prior fall-detection evaluation.

The staged-to-wild and synthetic-to-wild protocols are valuable. Results clearly expose the severe deployment-domain gap: models with strong controlled-domain performance remain much weaker on OF-In-the-Wild. This makes the benchmark useful even independently of the paper's claims about synthetic data.

The empirical finding that synthetic-only training attains higher wild-domain Fall F1 than staged-only training (64.2% versus 60.5–61.2%), with the combined set reaching 65.6%, is interesting and practically relevant. Timeline experiments further reveal a useful interaction between training domain and motion- versus appearance-oriented features.

The manuscript documents source licenses or permissions, dataset-specific splits, synthetic prompt factors, computational resources, and annotation workflow. Its discussion of privacy, surveillance, false alarms, generator bias, and human oversight is appropriate and strengthens the submission.

The paper is generally clear and visually effective, with extensive domain-distance tables, per-domain results, and supplementary embedding visualizations. The benchmark could have meaningful impact by reducing fragmented and overly optimistic evaluation in fall detection.
weaknesses: The classification methodology is internally inconsistent. Section 4 states that VideoMAE-K400 is fine-tuned end-to-end, and Tables 2–5 describe VideoMAE as being trained, whereas the appendix says that extracted backbone features are passed to a separate lightweight temporal transformer. This must be reconciled because it materially changes the interpretation and reproducibility of the results.

The construction of classification samples from densely labeled, variable-length recordings is insufficiently specified. The manuscript does not clearly explain window length, sampling, label assignment, overlap, treatment of transitions, class balancing, or video/frame-level metric aggregation. Exact ASQuery hyperparameters and several feature/distance implementation details are also missing.

The central comparisons use single runs without confidence intervals, seed variation, or significance testing. Consequently, the small gains of combined training over synthetic-only training (+1.4 Fall-F1 points) and some staged-versus-synthetic differences cannot confidently support broad superiority claims. The paper should temper statements that synthetic data can generally surpass real collections.

Synthetic-versus-staged comparisons are confounded by differences in dataset size, class distribution, clip duration, temporal complexity, scene composition, and outdoor content. The paper itself notes that OF-Synthetic and OF-In-the-Wild share outdoor activities. Controlled size-matched and factor-matched ablations would be needed to attribute improvements to demographic or synthetic diversity rather than these correlated factors.

Annotation quality assurance is described only qualitatively: nearly all videos received a second pass, but the exact coverage, independent annotator overlap, inter-annotator agreement, boundary tolerance, and adjudication statistics are absent. Transferring labels from one synchronized view to other views can also create view-specific errors when visibility or temporal alignment differs.

The claimed demographic controls are prompt-level attributes rather than validated subject attributes. Moreover, age groups deliberately use different environments and clothing, so the cross-age split conflates age with context; the reported degradation cannot be interpreted as age robustness. The use of race/ethnicity categories in generated prompts also deserves a more careful account of verification and stereotyping risks.

OF-In-the-Wild raises unresolved governance questions because it contains genuine accidents and potentially identifiable people sourced through OOPS. Citing the parent dataset's license is helpful, but the paper should clarify consent, redistribution rights for underlying web videos, de-identification, takedown procedures, and whether pretrained models may have encountered overlapping web content.

Baseline breadth is somewhat limited for a benchmark of this scale: classification relies on one principal representation/model pipeline and supervised segmentation on ASQuery with two feature types. Additional modern video baselines, simple binary fall baselines, and per-dataset/domain uncertainty would make the proposed benchmark and its conclusions more convincing.
